code.title: LSP: a Penguin that throws from fly() breaks callers

followUps: Usually Dependency Inversion (D), because it makes code testable, and testable code is what lets you apply every other principle safely. In legacy code with new MySqlClient() buried in methods, you cannot write a test, so you cannot refactor with confidence. Start by pulling database, HTTP and clock access behind small interfaces passed in through the constructor. Example: a 2,000-line OrderManager with no tests gets an OrderRepository interface; now a fake lets you pin its behaviour in a day. SRP and OCP splits follow safely after that.

Robert C. Martin ("Uncle Bob") collected the principles in his 2000 paper "Design Principles and Design Patterns", and Michael Feathers coined the acronym SOLID around 2004 by rearranging the initials. Martin had described each idea separately in the 1990s, and Barbara Liskov's substitution idea dates from 1987. So the acronym is about 20 years old, but the individual ideas are older.

code.title: SRP: a shared helper couples two actors

followUps: Ask who would request a change to this requirement, and group the behaviours by that person or team: that group is the actor. Take "the system calculates pay, reports hours and saves to the database". Pay belongs to finance, hours reports to HR, storage to the database team: three actors, so three reasons to change. Method: (1) list every behaviour, (2) write next to each the role that would ask for a change, (3) put behaviours with the same role together. If one stakeholder owns everything, one class is fine.

Accidental duplication is code that looks the same today but changes for different reasons, so merging it couples two actors. Example: finance and HR both compute regularHours = 40; if you share one helper and HR later changes it to 38, payroll silently changes too. Keeping two copies costs a few duplicated lines; the merge costs wrong paychecks. Merge only when the duplicated code would always change together, for the same actor.

code.title: OCP: add a payment method with one new class

followUps: It is a small violation in one place by design: some code has to know the concrete classes, and keeping that knowledge in a single composition root is the accepted trade-off. OCP says the business logic (the Checkout class) stays closed; the wiring file changes. With Spring's List<PaymentMethod> injection or ServiceLoader even that line disappears, because the framework discovers new classes. Aim to move change out of tested logic, not to make it zero.

Keep a switch when the set of cases is fixed and closed, for example the 4 suits of a card deck or the states of a sealed type. With Java sealed types or C# enums the compiler checks that every case is handled, so adding a case gives a compile error at each switch, which is exactly the safety you want. Use polymorphism when new types appear often; use a switch when new operations appear often. A short switch in one place beats 5 tiny classes.

code.title: LSP contract test run against every implementation

followUps: Covariant return types are an LSP-friendly feature: a subclass may return a more specific type, which is a stronger postcondition. If Animal create() is overridden by Dog create(), every caller expecting an Animal still gets one, plus more. The opposite, a less specific return, would break callers, so languages forbid it. Note that parameter types go the other way (contravariant): a subclass may accept a wider type, never a narrower one.

Yes, in the sense that matters: Collections.unmodifiableList(list) returns a List whose add throws UnsupportedOperationException, so code written for List breaks. Java chose practicality over a perfect hierarchy, and documents the exception as optional in the List contract. Cleaner designs (Kotlin's read-only List versus MutableList, or immutable collection types) split the interfaces so the bad call does not compile.

code.title: Square/Rectangle: immutable shapes avoid the broken promise
code.python:
# Square/Rectangle: mutable setters break LSP; immutable shapes have no promise to break.
class MutRect:
    def __init__(self): self.w = 0; self.h = 0
    def set_width(self, x): self.w = x
    def set_height(self, x): self.h = x
    def area(self): return self.w * self.h

class MutSquare(MutRect):  # keeps width == height, surprising the client
    def set_width(self, x): self.w = x; self.h = x
    def set_height(self, x): self.w = x; self.h = x

class Rect:
    def __init__(self, w, h): self.w = w; self.h = h
    def with_width(self, x): return Rect(x, self.h)  # returns a new object, no mutation
    def area(self): return self.w * self.h

class Sq:
    def __init__(self, s): self.side = s
    def area(self): return self.side * self.side

def client_area(r):
    r.set_width(5); r.set_height(4)
    return r.area()  # expects 20

print("Mutable Square: expected area 20, got %d" % client_area(MutSquare()))
shapes = [Rect(1, 4).with_width(5), Sq(4)]
print("Immutable: rectangle 5x4 area=%d, square 4x4 area=%d" % (shapes[0].area(), shapes[1].area()))

followUps: Because in code a rectangle comes with a promise that width and height can be changed independently, and a square cannot keep that promise. In maths nothing is ever mutated; in code setWidth(5) then setHeight(4) must give area 20. A square forces both sides equal, so the same client code returns 16 (the second setter overwrote the first). "Is-a" in OOP means "behaves like, in every use", not "is a special case in geometry".

Write one test for the Rectangle contract and run it against every subclass: set width 5, set height 4, assert that width is still 5 and area is 20. Rectangle passes; a mutable Square fails with area 16 because setting the height also changed the width. The failure is found at test time, not in production. This is the idea of a contract test suite: one abstract test class, one subclass per implementation.

code.title: ISP: small role interfaces for printer and scanner
code.python:
# ISP: small role interfaces so each client depends only on what it uses.
class SimplePrinter:  # needs no scan() or fax() stubs
    def print_doc(self, d): return "SimplePrinter prints: " + d

class OfficeMachine:  # one cohesive class, two roles
    def print_doc(self, d): return "OfficeMachine prints: " + d
    def scan(self, d): return "OfficeMachine scans: " + d

class PrintQueue:  # depends only on the print_doc role
    def __init__(self, printer): self.printer = printer
    def submit(self, doc): print(self.printer.print_doc(doc))

PrintQueue(SimplePrinter()).submit("report.pdf")
office = OfficeMachine()
PrintQueue(office).submit("memo.pdf")
print(office.scan("contract"))  # a scan client only calls scan()

followUps: A header interface is one interface that copies all public methods of a class (for example IOrderService with 40 methods); a role interface is a small one shaped by what one kind of client needs, such as OrderReader with 2 methods. Header interfaces give you mocking but little else, since every client still depends on all 40 methods. Role interfaces give real ISP: a reporting screen sees only OrderReader, and changes to checkout methods cannot break it. One class can implement many roles.

An interface is too small when callers must always use several together or when the pieces have no meaning alone, for example splitting a Stack into Pusher and Popper. A useful rule: shape the interface by one client's needs. If every client of A also uses B, merge them. If a test fake has to implement methods it never uses, or a client ignores half the methods, split. Typical size is 1 to 5 methods.

code.title: Constructor injection with a fake for tests
code.python:
# DI + DIP: OrderService depends on an abstraction it owns; the bottom of the file is the composition root.
class SmsNotifier:  # production adapter
    def send(self, user, msg): print("Production: SMS to %s: %s" % (user, msg))

class FakeNotifier:  # test double
    def __init__(self): self.sent = []
    def send(self, user, msg): self.sent.append(msg)

class OrderService:
    def __init__(self, notifier):  # constructor injection
        self.notifier = notifier
    def place(self, user, order_id):
        self.notifier.send(user, "order %d placed" % order_id)

OrderService(SmsNotifier()).place("ann", 7)  # wiring happens here only
fake = FakeNotifier()
OrderService(fake).place("ann", 7)  # same code, no real SMS
print("Test fake recorded %d message(s): %s" % (len(fake.sent), fake.sent[0]))

followUps: A composition root is the single place, usually main or the app start-up, where you create the concrete objects and connect them together. Everything else just receives its dependencies. Example: main builds new OrderService(new SqlOrderRepo(conn), new SmtpNotifier()) and runs it. Keeping all new calls for adapters here means business code never mentions MySQL or SMTP, and swapping them means editing one file.

A service locator is a global registry you ask for objects (Locator.get(Mailer.class)), so dependencies are hidden inside method bodies instead of shown in the constructor. You cannot tell what a class needs by reading its signature, tests must configure a global registry, and a missing registration fails at run time rather than at compile time. Constructor injection makes the same needs visible and checked. Locators are acceptable only inside the composition root or framework code.

code.title: Injected Clock and in-memory repository

followUps: Use mocks when what matters is the interaction itself, for example "the email was sent exactly once" or "the payment was never called when the cart is empty". Use fakes when you want realistic behaviour over many tests: an in-memory repository stores and returns real data, so tests read like the real system and survive refactoring. Mocks that script every call break when you change internals. Rule of thumb: fakes for state (repositories, clocks), mocks or spies for fire-and-forget side effects.

Run the same contract test suite against the fake and against the real adapter. Example: a test saves order 1, loads it back, expects the same data, and expects "not found" for id 99; it runs against InMemoryRepo in every build and against the real database in a slower integration job. If both pass, the fake is a valid substitute, which is LSP applied to test doubles. Without this, a fake can drift and tests pass while production fails.

YAGNI ("you ain't gonna need it") says do not build abstractions for needs you only imagine; OCP says be ready for change. They agree once you apply OCP to changes that have really happened. Start with a concrete class; when the second variation arrives, note it; at the third, extract the interface. Example: one payment method, write it directly; at the third (card, UPI, wallet) introduce PaymentMethod. Early abstraction guesses the wrong axis; late abstraction is cheap with tests.

CUPID (Dan North) says code should be Composable, follow the Unix philosophy, be Predictable, Idiomatic and Domain-based. Critics say SOLID is vague and invites over-engineering, with interfaces for everything. My view: the principles are good prompts for review, not laws. SRP and DIP pay off almost every time; OCP and ISP depend on real variation. I use SOLID as a checklist of questions ("who changes this? who depends on this?") and CUPID to keep code simple.

code.title: Facade over extracted classes (class-level strangler)
code.python:
# Strangler at class level: extract classes, keep the old God class as a delegating facade.
class TaxCalculator:  # extracted piece 1
    def with_tax(self, net): return net * 118 // 100

class InvoicePrinter:  # extracted piece 2
    def print_invoice(self, id, total): return "Invoice #%d: %d" % (id, total)

class LegacyBilling:  # old API unchanged, body now delegates
    def __init__(self):
        self.tax = TaxCalculator()
        self.printer = InvoicePrinter()
    def total(self, net): return self.tax.with_tax(net)
    def invoice(self, id, net): return self.printer.print_invoice(id, self.tax.with_tax(net))

legacy = LegacyBilling()  # old callers keep working
print("Legacy total(100) = %d" % legacy.total(100))
print("Legacy invoice(5,100) = " + legacy.invoice(5, 100))
# New code talks to the small class directly; old callers migrate one by one
print("New code uses TaxCalculator directly: %d" % TaxCalculator().with_tax(200))

followUps: Look at which files change together and who changes them: git log --format='%an' -- File.java | sort | uniq -c shows authors, and commit messages show the stakeholders ("tax rule", "report layout"). Two methods edited in different commits by different teams, for different tickets, belong to different actors. Example: 60 commits in a year, 35 mention "payroll" and 25 "HR report": two responsibilities, so extract two classes. Co-change analysis tools automate this counting.

The strangler fig pattern replaces an old system piece by piece while it keeps running. At class level: extract a new small class, make the old God class call it (a facade with the same public methods), and move callers over gradually. Example: LegacyBilling.total() now just returns taxCalculator.withTax(net). When no caller uses the legacy method any more, delete it. Every step ships on its own and is easy to revert.

code.title: Parking lot pricing with Strategy and Decorators
code.python:
# Parking lot pricing: a Strategy plus Decorators; new rules are new classes, ParkingService is untouched.
class Hourly:
    def price(self, h): return 10 * h

class Weekend:  # decorator: +50%
    def __init__(self, inner): self.inner = inner
    def price(self, h): return self.inner.price(h) * 3 // 2

class EvCharging:  # decorator: flat +20
    def __init__(self, inner): self.inner = inner
    def price(self, h): return self.inner.price(h) + 20

class ParkingService:
    def __init__(self, pricing): self.pricing = pricing  # DIP: depends on the abstraction
    def checkout(self, hours): return self.pricing.price(hours)

print("weekday 3h: %d" % ParkingService(Hourly()).checkout(3))
print("weekend 3h: %d" % ParkingService(Weekend(Hourly())).checkout(3))
print("weekend EV 3h: %d" % ParkingService(EvCharging(Weekend(Hourly()))).checkout(3))

followUps: Model each floor as a list of spots and pick the nearest free spot with a strategy object. Simple method: for each floor in order from the entry floor, scan its spots, and take the first free spot whose type fits the vehicle; or keep a min-heap of free spots per type ordered by (floor, distance). Heap pop is O(log N), the linear scan O(N). Put it behind SpotAllocator with a findSpot(vehicle) method so a "closest to the lift" rule is a new class, not an edit.

Concurrency matters in the step "find a free spot and mark it taken": two cars can be offered the same spot. Make that step atomic. Options: a lock around allocate (synchronized or a mutex) for one lot; a compare-and-set on each spot (tryOccupy() returns false if already taken, then try the next); or a database row lock or unique constraint if the lot is distributed. Keep the critical section tiny: only check and flip the flag, not payment or printing.

code.title: Retry decorator around a flaky payment adapter

followUps: A Decorator that wraps the payment adapter and retries on failure. The caller still sees a PaymentPort, so nothing else changes; this is OCP and DIP together. Steps: catch a transient error, wait (exponential backoff such as 100, 200, 400 ms), try again up to 3 times, then rethrow. Retry only safe operations, so send an idempotency key with the payment or you may charge twice. A circuit breaker decorator can be stacked on the same port.

Add an automated architecture test to the build so a violation fails the pull request. In Java use ArchUnit ("classes in domain must not depend on infra"); in Python import-linter contracts; in JavaScript dependency-cruiser rules; or split modules so the compiler refuses the import (separate Maven or Gradle modules, .NET projects). Start with one rule, domain depends on nothing outward, and keep it in CI so nobody can bypass it silently.

Automate the cheapest rules with the highest damage first: (1) the domain package must not import infrastructure or framework code (DIP), (2) no dependency cycles between packages, (3) a size limit such as 300 lines per class or 15 branches per switch (SRP, OCP). Then add naming rules, for example adapters live in infra and implement a port. Each rule is one test or lint line that fails the build, which gives an AI assistant instant feedback after its first draft.

Define a domain-owned port such as interface Summarizer { String summarize(String text); }, and write one adapter class that calls the vendor API and maps errors to domain errors. Business code takes the port in its constructor. In tests inject a fake that returns a fixed string (or throws a timeout) so the flow is fast, free and repeatable. Add a few contract tests against the real adapter in a separate job, and put retries, timeouts and logging in decorators around the port.
